newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico, U.S. to sign 10 agreements next week.
newsitem.headline: Mexico, U.S. to sign 10 agreements next week.

text.p: During U.S. President Bill Clinton's visit here next week Mexico and the United States will sign 10 agreements, including a pledge to fight money-laundering and the building of a new frontier bridge, Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria said on Friday.

Gurria told reporters that up to 14 U.S. Cabinet or Cabinet-level officials -- the largest number ever -- would come to Mexico for a meeting on Monday of the Binational Commission, a kind of joint annual U.S.-Mexico cabinet session which discusses bilateral issues.
Among the pacts to be signed would be an agreement for cooperation between the U.S. Treasury Department and the Mexican Finance Ministry to fight money laundering, Gurria said.

The accord will help train Mexican regulators in how to spot laundering activities and to deploy equipment that will automatically detect potentially suspicious transactions. Mexico, under heavy U.S. pressure, passed a law last year to make money laundering a crime.

Other agreements due to be signed next week include three for the protection of the environment, one for drug and alcohol tests for truck and bus drivers in the frontier area, and another for technical assistance for aviation.

Further pacts would cover the construction of a new frontier bridge in the Brownsville, Texas area, the widening of an existing one at Brownsville and the creation of a mechanism to improve security in frontier towns on both sides of the border, Gurria said.
The conclusions of the Binational Commission meetings would be presented formally to Clinton and Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo on Tuesday, he added.
Discussions between the two presidents would inevitably focus on what have long been the main issues concerning the United States and Mexico -- drugs, migration and trade, Gurria said.

On drugs, Gurria said the firing of the country's drug czar in February on narcotics corruption charges and the ensuing scandal had "really soured the mood" and led to "rather offensive statements" from some U.S. congressmen about Mexico's efforts against the cocaine cartels.
"We have to jump-start the confidence level, we have to get working together again, as we have no choice," he said.
Mexico is the largest single source of migrants to the United States and has been alarmed by recent U.S. moves to toughen rules and laws against illegal job-seekers.

"Not only have we had no convergent policies (on migration), we have had to some extent divergent policies," Gurria said. "Protection (of migrants) has been our leitmotif, interception has been the U.S. leitmotif."
"Clearly, we have to do better at finding a bilateral approach to the management of this issue."

Gurria said Clinton would be only the fifth U.S. president in history to visit the Mexican capital and the trip offered a "unique opportunity" for face-to-face contact and for the U.S. leader to get a personal impression of his southern neighbour.
"The president will take with him an image, an opinion, a feeling of what Mexico is about, of what Mexico stands for, of what Mexico means and can represent for the United States," Gurria said.
"The fact that the president of the United States is visiting Mexico already makes the visit a success."
